title: Sleeper Effect
hook: The claim sounds familiar weeks later, but the warning label that came with it has gone missing.
counterintuition: A weak source may not stay weak in memory; over time, the message can feel more credible as the source fades, so the decision needs the warning attached to the claim, not stored nearby.
tryThisNow: Find one claim you are about to use. Write its source beside it, then add one word of source quality before you let it influence the choice.
keyTakeaway: Treat familiar claims as unfinished evidence until the source comes back with them.

breakdown.fastRead: A court clerk sees an old budget number quoted in a custody debate. The number feels known, so it starts to sound true. Only later does she recall that it came from a draft marked weak. That is the sleeper effect: the claim stays while the source note fades. A claim can outlive its source. Protect the next choice by linking the bad-source note with the claim before familiar turns into trusted.
breakdown.deepRead:
A rumor arrives with a bad label. You hear it from a person who often exaggerates, or from a report that says the data is preliminary, or from a video clearly made to persuade. At first, the warning works. You discount the claim. Then two weeks pass, the source grows blurry, and the claim remains. It starts to feel like something you have known for a while.

That is the danger. Source memory is weaker than message memory in many real choices. You may remember that a supplier had defect problems and forget that the number came from a competitor. You may remember that a neighborhood was unsafe and forget that the story was a campaign mailer. You may remember that a treatment was risky and forget that the clip was built to frighten viewers. Familiarity can return wearing the clothes of truth.

Memory often keeps the message and drops the label.

The correction is to attach the label to the message before the delay does its work. Do not store the claim in one mental box and the source in another. Write them together: defect rate, unverified vendor rumor; rent estimate, landlord lobby sheet; safety concern, edited activist video. The point is not cynicism. Good sources deserve to travel with the claim too. The discipline is pairing.

This matters when decisions stretch over time. A claim heard on Monday may shape a vote on Friday. A vivid story read in a proposal may reappear in a budget meeting next month. If the source warning is not embedded in the notes, the sleeper effect gets a chance to choose for you. The fix is small and mechanical: keep source quality visible at the moment of decision.
breakdown.fullRead:
The warehouse tour smells of dust, new paint, and old forklift oil. A broker says the east loading bay floods twice a year, then shrugs when asked where the figure originated. The team discounts it during the tour. Three weeks later, in the lease meeting, the flooding line returns without the shrug attached. Nobody says, 'broker rumor.' They say, 'We know that bay floods.' The sentence has become cleaner with age.

This is delayed persuasion at work. A message can be discounted at first because its source is weak, biased, fictional, or openly persuasive. Later, the source tag decays faster than the message. What remains is familiarity, and familiarity is easily mistaken for evidence. The mind does not always retrieve the footnote with the fact. It retrieves the fact-shaped object and lets the room proceed.

Carl Hovland's work with the wartime film Why We Fight helped make this problem visible. The film was propaganda, and viewers could discount it as such, yet persuasion could grow after time had passed because the source and its warning lost force. Gareth Cook later described a similar television version of the problem: misinformation can gain power over time when the dubious origin becomes harder to recall. The mechanism is not mysterious. The label fades. The claim stays.

Which claims in your head have lost their tags?

A clean decision process treats source labels as part of the content. If a call log says a warehouse floods, the note should also say who said it, what their incentive was, and whether a public record confirms it. If a campaign mailer says a court policy saves money, the budget column should say campaign mailer, unverified, before the number moves into the calendar. If a social post claims a product defect, the review should tie the claim to the poster, the date, and the evidence behind it.

The hard part is that the sleeper effect does not feel like gullibility. It arrives as memory. You are not saying, 'I believe bad sources.' You are saying, 'I have heard this before.' That sentence can be useful when the source is good and repeated evidence exists. It becomes dangerous when the repetition comes from a weak origin that has been laundered by time. When the source is weak, attach the warning to the claim itself.

There is a limit. You cannot footnote every casual statement in daily life. Some claims are too small to track, and some sources are obvious enough in the moment. The point is to protect consequential choices: leases, custody schedules, product recalls, public budgets, hiring decisions, health claims, safety reviews. When the cost of being wrong is real, source memory needs help.

The best help is visible. Put the source in the same row as the claim. Color weak sources differently. Add 'unverified' to the phrase, not just to the document title. Ask, before the vote, 'What is the source on this?' If nobody can answer, the claim should drop back to rumor status until it earns its way forward. Familiarity is not a credential. It is only a feeling that something has passed through your mind before.

examples.title: The custody calendar with a stale number
examples.scenario: A budget column is highlighted in yellow on the family court calendar spreadsheet in a Boston courthouse workroom. Elizabeth, the scheduling coordinator, must decide whether to recommend a cheaper supervised-visit block after hearing the number repeated all week. She writes sleeper effect beside the column, adds 'campaign flyer, unverified' to the note, and asks finance for the source before the judge's clerk sees it.
examples.whatToDo: Attach source quality to the number before the familiar claim shapes the calendar.
examples.whyItMatters: The repeated budget figure can feel official after the weak source fades from memory.

examples.title: The defect review with a remembered rumor
examples.scenario: "Wasn't there a brake-hose issue?" the plant manager asks while a calendar invite for the auto-parts defect review blinks on the Windsor conference screen. Scott must decide whether to delay shipment based on a familiar claim from last month. He marks source memory risk on the invite, traces the claim to a competitor newsletter, and orders a same-day inspection instead of repeating the rumor as fact.
examples.whatToDo: Recover the source before a familiar defect claim becomes the basis for a shipment decision.
examples.whyItMatters: Source memory can fade while the defect story keeps its persuasive force.

examples.title: The lease meeting with an orphaned claim
examples.scenario: The call log crackles under Madeleine's thumb as she flips through broker notes in a Lyon warehouse office. She must decide between rejecting the east bay lease or checking the flood story that everyone now repeats. She writes Why We Fight beside the unverified broker line, reminds the team how persuasive claims can outlive labels, and requests municipal flood records before the vote.
examples.whatToDo: Treat a source-less remembered claim as unverified until it is tied to a record.
examples.whyItMatters: The warning attached to a persuasive claim can fade before the lease decision arrives.

examples.title: The breach room with an old warning
examples.scenario: You are standing beside a stamped form in the Dublin breach room while the incident board fills with red initials. Bruce, the security lead, must decide whether to block a vendor because a two-month-old claim says its logs are unsafe. He writes delayed persuasion on the form, asks who made the claim, and changes the action from vendor block to evidence review until the source is recovered.
examples.whatToDo: Pause a high-cost response when the claim is familiar but the source is missing.
examples.whyItMatters: Delayed persuasion can make an old warning feel solid just when a breach room wants speed.

examples.title: The volunteer plan with a repeated scare
examples.scenario: It took Katarina three planning meetings at the Rotterdam urban farm to notice that the same volunteer-safety scare kept returning without a source. The policy draft quoted a story from a neighborhood forum, but the forum post had been flagged as propaganda during the first review. She must decide whether to cut evening shifts. She marks the draft, restores the source warning, and asks for incident reports before changing the rota.
examples.whatToDo: Put the propaganda label back beside the story before it changes staffing policy.
examples.whyItMatters: A vivid story can keep persuading after the source warning has dropped out of the conversation.

examples.title: The warranty desk with a familiar complaint
examples.scenario: Why does the same floor sticker make every returned washer seem defective? Aman finds it under the appliance warranty desk in a London service center after the monthly postmortem. The sticker warns staff about one viral complaint from a year ago, but the source was a staged repair video. He writes sleeper on the sticker, removes it from the intake counter, and adds verified failure rates to the next claim review.
examples.whatToDo: Remove stale source-less cues from the workspace and replace them with verified rates.
examples.whyItMatters: A sleeper cue can keep influencing warranty decisions long after its origin is forgotten.

reviewCards.front: A claim feels familiar, but the source is missing. What source-quality check should return?
reviewCards.back: Find the source and rate its quality again. Familiarity can outlive the warning that made the claim suspect.

reviewCards.front: A weak source produced a vivid claim. What note protects the future decision?
reviewCards.back: Write the source label in the same line as the claim, such as 'unverified vendor rumor' or 'edited advocacy video.'

reviewCards.front: Why does repetition make sleeper-effect errors worse?
reviewCards.back: Repetition strengthens familiarity while the source tag may fade, making the claim feel cleaner than it is.

reviewCards.front: When should you spend time tracking sources?
reviewCards.back: Track sources for consequential choices where a false claim can move money, safety, reputation, or rights.

reviewCards.front: What should happen when nobody can identify a claim's source?
reviewCards.back: Move the claim back to rumor or unverified status until evidence earns it a place in the decision.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Attach source quality to claims before time turns familiarity into false authority.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I write down a claim that may affect a later choice, then I will write the source and source quality in the same line.
If a familiar claim appears without a source, then I will downgrade it to unverified until the source is recovered.
If a vivid story changes my view, then I will save the source label beside the claim before repeating it.
If someone says 'we know this,' then I will ask what the source is before the claim enters the decision.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one familiar claim in a current decision. Find its source, label its quality, and rewrite the note so the source cannot detach from the claim.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit one decision document for orphaned claims and add source labels before the next meeting.

memorableLines.text: A claim can outlive its source.
Memory often keeps the message and drops the label.
When the source is weak, attach the warning to the claim itself.
